entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Alveary Modern Language Lessons are designed to mirror the way children acquire their first language, using methods like gestures, picture recognition, songs, repeated phrases, and storytelling to create meaningful connections and context. These foundational approaches are seamlessly adapted to teach school-age children a second language.

The lessons are designed to be open-and-go with optional video/audio file support. They do not require any background in the target language for the parent/teacher or students. They only take about 15-20 min a day and can be easily adjusted to meet a variety of grade ranges from 1st to 6th grades.

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content: Three lessons each week are shared between Grades 1-6, but students in Grades 4-6 add two additional grammar lessons. This course is on a six-year rotation of lessons, so it is suitable for students who took Lower French last year or students just starting their studies.

blocks.text:
Students will complete a picture study lesson each week. Students will spend two weeks with the same vocabulary and narration sentences. Each lesson has an accompanying video to follow along with the lesson. In these lessons, students will be focused on beginning the skill of narration in another language within the context of discussing a picture from the assigned picture study book. They will use vocabulary and narration series sentences to help them describe what they see. Narration in another language generally follows this progression: 

- Recall - When given the French word, students should be able to identify the given word or phrase by pointing to a picture or making a gesture that demonstrates the word or phrase. 

- Recite - When given a prompt students will learn to respond in French. At this stage, students can be asked to say the narration series as they point to the corresponding image. Likewise they will practice saying the French word for a given image or gesture.

- Compose - As understanding grows, students may begin to notice objects in a picture or in the world around them and be able to describe them using French. Beginning French will be broken, often with improper grammar. That is ok. Much in the same way that children learn how to use proper tense and grammatical structure in speaking their first language, they will develop that here too, but at this stage it should be a byproduct of their learning, rather than the primary focus.

NOTE: While using these lessons and tools, keep the end goal in mind. Students should be working toward using the language to describe pictures in books and the world around them.

In grades 4-6, students are given the option of an additional extension day for picture study lessons. On these extension days, students will review the picture study lessons from the previous day. Students will also receive a gentle introduction to new grammar concepts every other week. Each lesson has an accompanying video to follow along.

Below is what you can expect for the general flow of a lesson:
- Read/watch any preparatory material and look over any student notebook pages or resources that will be used in the lesson. 
- Review the order of the lesson, and pull up any links that will be used in the lesson. 
- Practice the Phrase of the Week. 
- Ask students what they recall from the previous lesson.
- Play the video/audio links provided using the QR code or links page.
- Introduce and practice new vocabulary using TPR and picture recognition.
- Introduce and practice narration sentences, pointing to corresponding images.
For picture study lessons, students can find a Vocabulary Glossary in the reference section of their Student Notebook to follow along as new words are being introduced and for review.

Students will complete 1 literature lesson per week. In these lessons, your student will focus on building listening comprehension. When you first learn a new language, it can be hard to hear it and understand it at the same time. Here, students are encouraged to infer the meaning of a phrase or sentence without the pressure of needing to memorize each individual word and its various use cases. As you work with the vocabulary in these sections, remember that the goal is comprehension in context. The literature lessons have more difficult words and sentence structures in order to build students' ability to comprehend the whole. Students will benefit greatly from working with vocabulary cards in more of a sentence structure for these lessons. They can build the story lines with the vocabulary cards as you read and review, but don’t worry if they aren’t catching EVERY word. Many of the commonly used words may be hard to “see” in vocabulary card form, but with repetition, students will begin to recognize them. That is why we have also included storyline cards. Students can start to “see” parts of the storyline vocabulary as it is repeated in different contexts.

In grades 4-6, students are given the option of an additional extension day for literature lessons. These extension days give additional time to practice not just comprehending the story, but also saying it aloud and writing it through copywork in the target language to build familiarity with what the language looks like in written form. Each lesson has accompanying video or audio to follow along with.

Below is what you can expect for the general flow of a lesson:
- Read/watch any preparatory material and look over any student notebook pages to familiarize yourself.
- Choose a few sentences, words, or vocabulary cards to review at the beginning of each lesson.
- Press play on the video/audio link provided in the QR link page.
- Introduce new vocabulary (pause as needed).
- Practice TPR vocabulary.
- Read the story.
- Practice storyline recognition and building.
- Work on storyboards or copywork.

On the literature pages of the student notebook, you will find images for any new vocabulary for the week and a storyboard box for students to draw their narrations. Copywork lines have also been provided for students to write the story lines on extension days. Copywork extension days are only scheduled for Grades 4-6.

Students will complete 1 Songs, Rhymes, & Conversations lesson per week. In these lessons, students are exposed to cultural songs and rhymes and also given the opportunity to practice singing or saying the language out loud in a fun and engaging way. Students can often feel self-conscious or silly when trying to speak a new language, and by using songs & rhymes, we can help them overcome that hurdle. This lesson does not have a video. Instead, it gives teachers step-by-step instructions on how to lead the lesson and includes suggested accompanying audio to follow as you learn the song or rhyme. Students will also begin to learn a few conversational phrases they can use in the target language during these lessons. There are accompanying audio and conversation cards to aid in this part of the lesson.

Below is what you can expect for the general flow of a lesson:
- Read/watch any preparatory material and look over any student notebook pages to familiarize yourself.
- Choose a few sentences, words, or vocabulary cards to review at the beginning of each lesson.
- Open to the current song/rhyme.
- Press play on the video/audio link provided in the QR link page.
- Practice reciting/singing the passage.
- Listen to the audio introduction of new conversation phrases (pause as needed).
- Practice conversation recognition and building.

All of the songs have been provided at the front of the student notebook in order to aid in your students' ability to find them easily. For the conversational part of the lessons, it is suggested that students work in pairs. If that is not a possibility, then we recommend students use stuffed animals or puppets to practice this piece. There are no images for the conversation cards in the student notebooks. The conversation cards are for the teacher's benefit and for fun with building conversations as students progress in their speaking abilities.

➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Haussmann Architecture
Walking through Paris, one takes notice of the buildings lining many of the streets. Tall, rectangular buildings, built with beige stone and iron balconies were created by George-Eugène Haussmann in the latter half of the 1800s. Dive deeper into how and why this renovation happened. 


∞ Video Link: [George-Eugène Haussmann - Architecture](https://classroom.ricksteves.com/videos/paris-haussmann-buildings-and-grand-boulevards) 
∞ Video Link : [George-Eugène Haussmann - Life History](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xUcvsqcD7ww)

lessons.grammarInstructions: In French, nouns are either “masculine” or “feminine”. Some clues indicating if a noun is masculine or feminine is the use of the articles. There are definite and indefinite articles. Singular definite articles include "le/la/l'". "Le" is masculine singular. "La" is feminine singular. "L'" is used before a noun that begins with a vowel and mute h. Singular indefinite articles include "un/une". "Un" is masculine singular. "Une" is feminie singular.

The partitive article (some, any)
In English, partitive articles are often omitted. For example, 'We have pens and paper." can be said instead of "We have some pens and some paper." In French, the word /some/ must never be omitted and it is expressed by the word /of the/ (some bread = of the bread).

Feminine singular = de la / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Masculine and feminine singular = des

grammarCharts.extraInstructions:
The partitive article (some, any)
In English, partitive articles are often omitted. For example, 'We have pens and paper." can be said instead of "We have some pens and some paper." In French, the word /some/ must never be omitted and it is expressed by the word /of the/ (some bread = of the bread).
Masculine singular = du / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Feminine singular = de la / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Masculine and feminine singular = des

grammarCharts.name: Masculine | Feminine
grammarCharts.extraInstructions: In French, nouns are either “masculine” or “feminine”. Some clues indicating if a noun is masculine or feminine is the use of the articles. lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Months of the year, Part 1
The months of the year (les mois de l'année) in French are masculine, generally not capitalized, and similar to English.  They are: janvier January), février (February), mars (March), avril (April), mai (May), juin (June), julliet(July), août (August), septembre (September), octobre (October), novembre (November) and décembre (December).

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Question words
French question words (les mots interrogatifs) are essential for forming questions. The end of a question has the same question mark as in English.

lines.translation: without some plausible excuse.

lines.translation: So he cast about for a grievance and said at last,

lines.translation: "Last year, sir, you grossly insulted me."
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 27

lines.sentence: "C'est impossible, monsieur." l'agneau a bêlé,
lines.translation: "That is impossible, sir." bleated the Lamb,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 28

lines.sentence: "car je n'étais pas encore né."
lines.translation: "for I wasn't born then."
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 28

lines.sentence: "Eh bien," rétorquait le Loup, "tu te nourris dans mes prés."
lines.translation: "Well," retorted the Wolf, "you feed in my pastures."

lines.translation: "That cannot be," replied the Lamb,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 29

lines.sentence: "Car je n'ai jamais rien bu mis à part le lait de ma mère."
lines.translation: "For I have never yet drunk anything by my mother's milk."
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 29

lines.sentence: "Enfin bref," dit le loup,
lines.translation: "Well anyhow," said the Wolf,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 29

lines.sentence: "Je n'y vais pas sans mon repas,"
lines.translation: "I'm not going without my dinner,"
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 30

lines.sentence: et il a sauté sur l'agneau
lines.translation: and he sprang upon the Lamb
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 30

lines.sentence: et l'a dévoré sans plus de cérémonie.
lines.translation: and devoured it without more ado.

lines.sentence: qu'il le pouvait en l'air.
lines.translation: as he could into the air.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 3

lines.sentence: Mais tout cela n'a servi a rien,
lines.translation: But it was all in vain,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 3

lines.sentence: car ils étaient juste hors d'atteinte.
lines.translation: for they were just out of reach.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 3

lines.sentence: il a donc abandonné
lines.translation: So he gave up trying
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 4

lines.sentence: et s'éloignait avec un air
lines.translation: and walked away with an air
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 4

lines.sentence: de la dignité et d'insouciance
lines.translation: of dignity and unconcern,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 4

lines.sentence: remarquant, "J'ai pensé
lines.translation: remarking, "I thought
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 5

lines.sentence: que ces raisons étaient mûrs,
lines.translation: those Grapes were ripe,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 5

lines.sentence: mais maintenant je vois
lines.translation: but I see now
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 5

lines.sentence: qu'ils sont assez aigres."
lines.translation: they are quite sour."
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 5

lines.sentence: Deux chèvres orgueilleuses se sont rencontrées
lines.translation: Two proud goats happened to meet
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 21

lines.sentence: sur les falaises opposées d'une haute chaîne de montagnes
lines.translation: on the opposite cliffs of a high mountain range
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 21

lines.sentence: où une rivière impétueuse coulait en dessous
lines.translation: where a fierce river ran below
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 21

lines.sentence: à travers une vallée rocheuse.
lines.translation: through a rocky valley.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 22

lines.sentence: Le seul pont pour traverser le ravin
lines.translation: The only bridge across the chasm
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 22

lines.sentence: était un arbre tombé si étroit
lines.translation: was a fallen tree so narrow
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 22

lines.sentence: au point d'effrayer deux souris qui se croisent
lines.translation: as to frighten two mice passing each other
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 23

lines.sentence: en même temps.
lines.translation: at the same time.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 23

lines.sentence: avaient l'impression d'avoir
lines.translation: felt that they had
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 23

lines.sentence: Les deux chèvres têtues
lines.translation: Both stubborn Goats
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 23

lines.sentence: le droit de traverser la rivière en permier;
lines.translation: the right to cross the river first;
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 24

lines.sentence: en posant un sabot à la fois
lines.translation: so setting one hoof at a time
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 24

lines.sentence: sur le fin tronc,
lines.translation: upon the slender log,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 24

lines.sentence: elles se trouvaient tête à tête
lines.translation: they found themselves head to head
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 24

lines.sentence: au milieu du pont.
lines.translation: in the middle of the bridge.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 25

lines.sentence: Aucune des deux chèvres ne voulait céder à l'autre,
lines.translation: Neither Goat would give way to the other,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 25

lines.sentence: et finalement elle sont tombées tous les deux
lines.translation: and finally they both fell
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 25

lines.sentence: la tête la première dans l'eau tumultueuses en bas.
lines.translation: headlong into the roaring waters below.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 25

lines.sentence: Un loup a décidé de se déguiser pour qu'
lines.translation: A Wolf resolved to disguise himself in order that
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 6

lines.sentence: il puisse s'attaquer à un troupeau de moutons
lines.translation: he might prey upon a flock of sheep
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 6

lines.sentence: sans crainte d'être détecté
lines.translation: without fear of detection,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 6

lines.sentence: il s'est revetu donc d'une peau de mouton
lines.translation: so he clothed himself in a sheepskin
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 7

lines.sentence: et s'est glissé parmi les moutons
lines.translation: and slipped among the sheep
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 7

lines.sentence: lorsqu'ils étaient au pâturage.
lines.translation: when they were out at pasture.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 7

lines.sentence: Il a complètement trompé le berger,
lines.translation: He completely deceived the shepherd,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 8

lines.sentence: et lorsque le troupeau fut parqué pour la nuit,
lines.translation: and when the flock was penned for the night,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 8

lines.sentence: il fut enfermé avec les autres
lines.translation: he was shut in with them.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 8

lines.sentence: Mais cette nuit-là, comme le hasard l'a voulu,
lines.translation: But that very night, as it happened,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 9

lines.sentence: le berger, ayant besoin de mouton pour la table,
lines.translation: the shepherd, requiring a supply of mutton for the table,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 9

lines.sentence: a mis ses mains sur le loup,
lines.translation: laid his hands on the wolf,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 9

lines.sentence: le prenait pour une brebis,
lines.translation: mistaking him for a sheep,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 10

lines.sentence: et il l'a achevé
lines.translation: and he finished him off
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 10

lines.sentence: avec son couteau sur place
lines.translation: with his knife on the spot.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 10

lines.sentence: Une tortue mécontent avec
lines.translation: A Tortoise, discontented with
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 16

lines.sentence: sa vie misérable et envieuse
lines.translation: a lowly life and envious
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 16

lines.sentence: des oiseaux qu'elle voyait s'amuser
lines.translation: of the birds that he saw enjoying themselves
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 16

lines.sentence: en air,
lines.translation: in the air,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 17

lines.sentence: a supplié un aigle
lines.translation: begged an Eagle
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 17

lines.sentence: de lui apprendre à voler.
lines.translation: to teach him to fly.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 17

lines.sentence: L'aigle a protesté qu'il était vain pour lui d'essayer,
lines.translation: The Eagle protested that it was idle for him to try,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 18

lines.sentence: comme la nature ne l'avait pas doté d'ailes
lines.translation: as nature had not provided him with wings;
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 18

lines.sentence: mais la Tortue l'a pressé de prières et de promesses de trésor,
lines.translation: but the Tortoise pressed him with entreaties and promises of treasure,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 18

lines.sentence: en insistant que ce n'était qu'une question d'
lines.translation: insisting that it could only be a question of
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 18

lines.sentence: apprendre l'art du pilotage.
lines.translation: learning the craft of the air.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 19

lines.sentence: enfin l'aigle finit donc par consentir
lines.translation: So at length the Eagle consented
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 19

lines.sentence: à faire le mieux qu'il pourrait pour lui
lines.translation: to do the best he could for him
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 19

lines.sentence: et l'a pris par ses serres.
lines.translation: and picked him up in his talons.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 19

lines.sentence: De s'envoler avec lui à une grande hauteur dans le ciel
lines.translation: Soaring with him to a great height in the sky
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 20

lines.sentence: puis il l'a laché
lines.translation: he then let him go,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 20

lines.sentence: et la miserable Tortue
lines.translation: and the wretched Tortoise
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 20

lines.sentence: est tombée la tete la premiere dans la mer.
lines.translation: fell headlong into the sea.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 20

lines.sentence: Un loup a rencontré un agneau
lines.translation: A wolf came upon a Lamb
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 26

lines.sentence: qui s'éloignait du troupeau
lines.translation: straying from the flock
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 26

lines.sentence: et éprouvait une certaine réticence à propos de
lines.translation: and felt some reluctance about
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 26

lines.sentence: l'idée de prendre la vie d'une créature impuissante.
lines.translation: taking the life of the helpless creature
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 26

lines.sentence: sans une raison plausible.
lines.translation: without some plausible excuse.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 27

lines.sentence: Il cherche donc un prétexte et dit finalement,
lines.translation: So he cast about for a grievance and said at last,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 27

lines.sentence: "L'année dernière, monsieur, vous m'avez insulté gravement."
lines.translation: "Last year, sir, you grossly insulted me."
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 27

lines.sentence: "C'est impossible, monsieur." l'agneau a bêlé,
lines.translation: "That is impossible, sir." bleated the Lamb,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 28

lines.sentence: "car je n'étais pas encore né."
lines.translation: "for I wasn't born then."
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 28

lines.sentence: "Eh bien," rétorquait le Loup, "tu te nourris dans mes prés."
lines.translation: "Well," retorted the Wolf, "you feed in my pastures."
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 28

lines.sentence: "Ce n'est pas possible," a répondu l'agneau,
lines.translation: "That cannot be," replied the Lamb,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 29

lines.sentence: "Car je n'ai jamais rien bu mis à part le lait de ma mère."
lines.translation: "For I have never yet drunk anything by my mother's milk."
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 29

lines.sentence: "Enfin bref," dit le loup,
lines.translation: "Well anyhow," said the Wolf,
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 29

lines.sentence: "Je n'y vais pas sans mon repas,"
lines.translation: "I'm not going without my dinner,"
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 30

lines.sentence: et il a sauté sur l'agneau
lines.translation: and he sprang upon the Lamb
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 30

lines.sentence: et l'a dévoré sans plus de cérémonie.
lines.translation: and devoured it without more ado.
lines.label: French Story Lines - Set 30

lessons.grammarInstructions: In French, nouns are either “masculine” or “feminine”. Some clues indicating if a noun is masculine or feminine is the use of the articles. There are definite and indefinite articles. Singular definite articles include "le/la/l'". "Le" is masculine singular. "La" is feminine singular. "L'" is used before a noun that begins with a vowel and mute h. Singular indefinite articles include "un/une". "Un" is masculine singular. "Une" is feminie singular.

lessons.grammarInstructions:
The partitive article (some, any)
In English, partitive articles are often omitted. For example, 'We have pens and paper." can be said instead of "We have some pens and some paper." In French, the word /some/ must never be omitted and it is expressed by the word /of the/ (some bread = of the bread).
Masculine singular = du / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Feminine singular = de la / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Masculine and feminine singular = des

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Partitive articles
The partitive article (some, any)
In English, partitive articles are often omitted. For example, 'We have pens and paper." can be said instead of "We have some pens and some paper." In French, the word /some/ must never be omitted and it is expressed by the word /of the/ (some bread = of the bread).
Masculine singular = du / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Feminine singular = de la / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Masculine and feminine singular = des

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Days of the Week
Days of the week in French (les jours de la semaine). Unlike in English, the days of the week in Frenchh do not begin with capital letters. Days of the week in French are masculine & singular - lundi (Monday), mardi (Tuesday), mercredi (Wednesday), jeudi (Thursday), vendredi (Friday), samedi (Saturday), dimanche (Sunday)

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Plural Nouns
In French, plural nouns are formed by adding -s with few exceptions. If the noun already ends in -s in the singular, no addition is necessary. 

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Partitive articles
The partitive article (some, any)
In English, partitive articles are often omitted. For example, 'We have pens and paper." can be said instead of "We have some pens and some paper." In French, the word /some/ must never be omitted and it is expressed by the word /of the/ (some bread = of the bread).
Masculine singular = du / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Feminine singular = de la / de l' (before vowels and mute h)
Masculine and feminine singular = des

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Nouns & Gender
In French, nouns are either “masculine” or “feminine”. Some clues indicating if a noun is masculine or feminine is the use of the articles. There are definite and indefinite articles. Singular definite articles include "le/la/l'". "Le" is masculine singular. "La" is feminine singular. "L'" is used before a noun that begins with a vowel and mute h. Singular indefinite articles include "un/une". "Un" is masculine singular. "Une" is feminie singular.  


➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Days of the Week
Days of the week in French (les jours de la semaine). Unlike in English, the days of the week in Frenchh do not begin with capital letters. Days of the week in French are masculine & singular - lundi (Monday), mardi (Tuesday), mercredi (Wednesday), jeudi (Thursday), vendredi (Friday), samedi (Saturday), dimanche (Sunday)

➜ EXAMPLES

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Numerals 1-10
Learn the numerals in French from 1-10. 
un (one), deux (two), trois (three), quatre (four), cinq (five), six (six), sept (seven), huit (eight), neuf (nine), dix (ten)


➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Subject pronouns
French subject pronouns replace nouns to indicate who or what is performing an action, similar to English ("I," "you," "he/she"). However, unlike English pronouns, they account for gender and levels of formality as well. "He/she" in English also are used to replace all nouns, not just people like in English. (This is just an introduction, there is more to learn about French pronouns.)

➜ EXAMPLES

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Adjectives & Agreements
In French, adjectives must agree with the nouns to which they refer. We look at the endings of the adjective to determine whether it is masculine or feminine, singular or plural. Adjectives that are masculine singluar stay as they are. Adjectives that are feminine singular have an -e added to them unless there is already an e. Masculine and feminine adjectives when plural had an -s added to them.

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Sentence Structure
French sentence structure follows the Subject + Verb + Object (SVO) pattern, simliar to English. There are some expections to this pattern but we will begin here. 

➜ EXAMPLES

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Numerals 1-10
Learn the numerals in French from 1-10. 
un (one), deux (two), trois (three), quatre (four), cinq (five), six (six), sept (seven), huit (eight), neuf (nine), dix (ten)


➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Adjectives & Agreements
In French, adjectives must agree with the nouns to which they refer. We look at the endings of the adjective to determine whether it is masculine or feminine, singular or plural. Adjectives that are masculine singluar stay as they are. Adjectives that are feminine singular have an -e added to them unless there is already an e. Masculine and feminine adjectives when plural had an -s added to them.

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Subject pronouns
French subject pronouns replace nouns to indicate who or what is performing an action, similar to English ("I," "you," "he/she"). However, unlike English pronouns, they account for gender and levels of formality as well. "He/she" in English also are used to replace all nouns, not just people like in English. (This is just an introduction, there is more to learn about French pronouns.)

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Sentence Structure
French sentence structure follows the Subject + Verb + Object (SVO) pattern, simliar to English. There are some expections to this pattern but we will begin here. 

➜ EXAMPLES

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - La baguette 
La baguette is a traditional type of bread eaten all over France. French people buy baguette from a boulangerie (bakery) daily to enjoy for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Traditional baguettes have only 4 ingredients. Discover more about how this French food is made. 

∞ Video Link: [La Baguette](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KURH-UeAN8A)

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Months of the year, Part 1
The months of the year (les mois de l'année) in French are masculine, generally not capitalized, and similar to English.  They are: janvier January), février (February), mars (March), avril (April), mai (May), juin (June), julliet(July), août (August), septembre (September), octobre (October), novembre (November) and décembre (December).

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Question words
French question words (les mots interrogatifs) are essential for forming questions. The end of a question has the same question mark as in English. 

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Months of the year, Part 2
The months of the year (les mois de l'année) in French are masculine, generally not capitalized, and similar to English.  They are: janvier January), février (February), mars (March), avril (April), mai (May), juin (June), julliet(July), août (August), septembre (September), octobre (October), novembre (November) and décembre (December).
